P1.evidence: The best open in the batch. The setter handoff was acknowledged and the duplication pre-empted in one move: 'I already got some information from Kim, could be that I ask the same questions just because I want to get the whole picture clear.' He then proved he had read the notes at two later points — 'I also heard that you're having sort of bad posture at work because you have a desk job' and 'I also saw, of course, you sort of noted down that you want to have longevity and energy' — which is exactly the 'so they feel seen' intent of the check. Frame agreement was sought and given, and the open question ran with the prospect's name attached. The frame itself is the recurring weak point: two parts plus the disqualification clause, with 'what's in the way' and 'what you need' still absent.

P2.evidence: Strong across most of the phase. Height was asked directly; age and weight came from the setter notes and were confirmed only in the recap. Work was covered — the desk job and its postural consequence early, and the actual occupation later, though not until 00:54:50, after the deal had already slipped. The injury enquiry was the standout: 'do you feel like you also have something with immobility or inflexibility at the moment?' opened the whole cascading back history, and the rep followed up properly on how it was resolved, whether it is constant, and what remains. Training frequency, results and diet were all thorough, the diet detail extending to meal kits, protein scoops, calorie banking and the eating window. Energy was asked directly and produced a genuinely useful observation about coffee and sluggishness. Two gaps: health conditions were never asked as such, so everything medical arrived because the prospect volunteered it; and sleep was never raised at all, in a call with a single father of two young children.

P3.evidence: Competent on the surface and thin at the bottom. The visual goal was pinned down properly — 'just overall, like visually, what's the goal? Do you want to have abs? you want to be ripped?' — and mobility, energy and longevity were all covered. The future-state question ran and landed the best line in the call: 'it would feel like a lifestyle and identity shift... it would be a new way of life.' The recap was long, accurate and confirmed. But the scripted bridge was never asked in its own right; the nearest thing was asking what he meant by longevity, a term he had already written on his application. And the who-else question was supplied rather than asked — 'And probably also maybe be a bad, even a better role model for your kids as well, right?' — which produced only a lukewarm 'it's something I might consider and think about for sure'. A drive that the prospect does not own is not a drive.

P4.evidence: Well run. History was opened with a clean question — 'is it that you've gone up and down with fitness-wise, or has it always stayed something that you have been doing?' — which produced the trainer five or six years ago, the marathons, COVID, the children and the climb to 200 lb. The plateau pattern came out clearly. The blocker question was the best moment of the phase: 'do you feel like there's anything that would stop you from being successful in phase two?... do you feel like there's anything internally for you that would stop you?' The answer, 'Honestly, just an injury at this point', is both the answer to the check and the most clinically significant sentence in the call, and it was not followed up. The gap was named by the prospect himself: 'I just don't know a kettlebell routine, and I just don't know about form with kettlebells, so I think that has been the main driver.' Marked down because 'why do you feel it didn't stick' was never put, and the 'information isn't the problem' challenge was absent.

P5.evidence: Absent in its entirety. The rep ran the positive future projection at 00:23:53 and went straight from it into the pre-pitch. There is no negative projection, no two-year horizon, no settle question, no 'why not', and no line in the sand anywhere in fifty-five minutes. This matters more here than on most calls because the prospect's own programme is currently working: he is 20 lb down and progressing without help, and he said so — 'I'm doing well enough with my own cutting. The program is well enough... at least to get me to the next 30, 60 days.' Without a cost of inaction, waiting 60 days was the obviously rational choice and the rep had nothing to set against it. Notably the coaching one-to-one that reviewed this call an hour later focused entirely on the pitch and did not identify the missing phase.

P6.evidence: The isolation sequencing was handled well and better than on most calls in this batch. The belief check ran twice, before and after the presentation. The cost variable was then isolated explicitly before the number was given — a 1-to-10 scale returned 'an easy seven... And that will move based on cost', and the rep followed with 'outside of the cost aspect, do you feel like, yeah, this is something I see myself doing?', answered 'Yeah, I could totally do it.' That is the isolation working correctly and it correctly predicted the shape of the objection. P6c is a partial because the script asks for a clear yes and a seven is not one; with no Phase 5 to return to, the hesitation had nowhere to go. One phrasing to correct, which the manager also flagged in the review: 'is there anything else that you would need from our side?' invites the prospect to invent requirements and undercuts the certainty the phase is meant to build.

P11.evidence: Price was presented and a plan was structured, but the prospect deferred and no agreement was reached, so none of the payment or onboarding steps became reachable.

objection_plays.detail: The strongest run of the isolation half in the batch. Isolation ran before the number and again after it. The hypothetical ran and confirmed intent: 'let's say 9K Canadian would now fall on your lap, would you be like, okay, Richard, let's get started' — 'Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah.' The SHOULD-versus-HOW distinction ran in substance and returned the right answer: 'do you really think that thinking about is going to make a big difference or is it going to boil down to seeing how you could make it work?' — 'It's going to boil down to seeing how I can make it work.' The pay-upfront-but-we-can-break-it-up move ran and produced an actual structured plan plus third-party financing, which the prospect declined. What did not run is the entire financial picture: no question about cash on hand, monthly surplus after bills, number of credit cards, available credit, or used versus available. Most strikingly, crypto, stocks and investments were never raised with a prospect who works in the financial markets and had just disclosed 12 to 15 months of liquid runway. The one asset class the script explicitly names was the one this prospect was most likely to hold.

Triggered by 'give me the time to think about it' and 'I'm going to sit on it'. The deciding-versus-thinking move ran and worked. The 'can this get you to your goal' check ran in a variant form — 'Do you feel like it comes down to wanting to make sure that you get your bang for your buck?' — and was answered no, the value is there. But the play stopped there. No 'so what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started?' beyond the money, no 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision?', no identity question, and no final 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?'. The prospect also named the play as it was being run — 'you're doing your role now and you're doing your role against someone who's done it for you know 20 years' — which is worth noting for coaching: scripted moves land badly on a sixteen-year sales veteran.

Present in substance and stated plainly at the close: 'The timing is just not right for me. It really boils down to that.' One scripted move ran, and ran well — the cost of delay, framed against his actual problem rather than generically: 'delaying it isn't going to change anything, right?... when it comes to doing like sort of the waiting another 60 days, when do you know when to stop cutting? Maybe it's too much. When are you going to figure that out?' That is the right question and it went unanswered. The rest of the play did not run: no 'things never slow down', no 'when does it actually become the right time', and no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets'. The rep then chose explicitly not to press — 'I'd rather have you not do it if it's going to put you in a financial position' — which given no income and two dependent children is a defensible judgement rather than a failure.

notes: Two genuinely good halves and a hole in the middle. The open, the injury enquiry, the blocker question and the pre-price isolation were all among the best work in the batch, and the rep's decision not to press a prospect with no income and two children is the right instinct. But the Consequence Frame is entirely absent, which is fatal against a prospect whose own free programme is visibly working — waiting 60 days cost him nothing and the rep gave him no reason it did. When the objection arrived he reached for pricing improvisation instead: a $200 monthly surcharge and an invented first-month exit. Coach on running P5 against self-sufficient prospects, and on running the financial picture — a man in the financial markets with 15 months of runway was never asked a single question about investments.
